engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Opening Principle #3: Castle Early
chess.body: King safety is non-negotiable in the opening. Castle within the first 10 moves. An uncastled king in the centre is a target. After castling, your king is protected by 3 pawns and 2 corner squares. Rooks also connect after castling. Rule: castle before you attack.

book.author: Carol Dweck
book.chapter: Fixed vs Growth Mindset: The Belief That Changes Everything
book.lesson: Dweck's 30 years of research found that children (and adults) hold one of two fundamental beliefs about their abilities. Fixed mindset: abilities are innate — you're either smart or you're not. This leads to avoiding challenges (to avoid looking dumb), giving up when things get hard, and feeling threatened by others' success. Growth mindset: abilities develop through dedication and hard work. This leads to embracing challenges, persisting through setbacks, and finding inspiration in others' success. The most important finding: the mindset is not fixed. It can be changed by learning about it.
book.key_quote: The belief that your abilities are fixed is the only thing that makes them fixed.
book.action: Notice your self-talk after a failure today. Is it fixed ('I'm not good at this') or growth ('I haven't learned this yet')? The word 'yet' is the most powerful in the growth mindset.
crux: Two mindsets: fixed (abilities are static) and growth (abilities develop through effort).
Fixed mindset makes every task a verdict on your worth, so it avoids risk.
Growth mindset treats effort and failure as the mechanism of improvement.
Praising talent produces fragility. Praising process produces resilience.
'Not yet' is the most useful phrase in learning.
Fixed mindset avoids challenges that might reveal limits — and so never finds them.
Effort is what talent requires, not a substitute for it.
Criticism is data in a growth mindset and an attack in a fixed one.
Others' success is inspiration in one frame, threat in the other.
Mindsets are domain-specific. You can be growth-oriented at work and fixed about maths.
Fixed-mindset relationships expect compatibility; growth-mindset relationships expect work.
CEO disease: fixed-mindset leaders need to be the smartest person and suppress bad news.
You can change mindset by noticing the fixed voice and answering it deliberately.
learnings: How you explain a failure determines whether you get anything from it.
Talent praise is a trap. Process praise builds durability.
Avoiding challenge to protect self-image caps growth permanently.
'Not yet' converts a verdict into a timeline.
examples: Dweck's students given 'you're smart' avoided harder puzzles; those praised for effort chose them and improved.
Michael Jordan was cut from varsity and became famous for practice volume, not gifts.
Lee Iacocca's fixed mindset at Chrysler: early success, then defensiveness, suppressed dissent, and decline.
adapt: The trading ledger is a learning instrument, not a verdict. -0.029R on 1H is information, not judgement.
Rejection from a Dubai role is 'not yet' with a specific gap. Name the gap.
Praise your daughter's effort and persistence, not how clever she is. It starts this early.
The 8/8 APEX stop-outs were a diagnosis of the exit rule, not of your ability.

father.title: Point at things
father.do: Point at an object and name it, then look at her to check she followed your finger.
father.why: Following a point is a joint-attention milestone that typically emerges between 9 and 12 months. Practising the gesture now builds toward it, and delayed joint attention is one of the earlier developmental flags worth knowing about.

father.why: Self-directed narration builds the vocabulary of internal states. It is the same mechanism as labelling emotions, applied to actions first because they are observable.

interview_tech.q: Gross margin fell 180bps. Walk me through the bridge.
interview_tech.a: Decompose into four drivers: mix — did the sales split shift toward lower-margin categories; price — did you discount more, measured as markdown as a percent of gross sales; cost — did landed cost rise from FX, freight or supplier price; and shrink/wastage. Quantify each in basis points so they sum to 180. The bridge is the answer, not the total. In retail the most common culprit is markdown depth on aged stock, which is really an buying error surfacing one season late.

interview_tech.q: Auditors propose an adjustment you disagree with. What do you do?
interview_tech.a: Separate judgement from fact. If it is a factual error, show the evidence and it goes away. If it is a judgement — provisioning, impairment, lease term — set out your basis in a technical memo: the standard, the specific paragraph, the assumptions and their support. Escalate to the engagement partner if needed, and involve the audit committee chair early rather than late. If they still disagree and it is material, you record it. What you never do is trade an adjustment against a different one.

interview_soft.q: Describe a time you had to deliver bad news to senior stakeholders.
interview_soft.a: Lead with the structure you used, because that is the skill. Bad news goes: the number, the cause, the impact, the plan, the ask. No preamble. Deliver it early even when incomplete — 'here is what I know now and what I will know Friday' beats a complete answer a week late. Give a specific example with the actual figure and what you did next. The tell they look for: did you surface it or did someone else find it.

interview_soft.q: Why should we hire you over a candidate with Big Four and listed-company experience?
interview_soft.a: Do not disparage the alternative. Frame the trade: audit teaches you to verify what happened; operating finance teaches you to change what happens next. Then be specific about what you own that they do not — a live multi-country P&L, an ERP implementation you led rather than advised on, and store-level decisions you made and were held to. End with the honest gap and how you would close it. Confidence with a named weakness beats confidence alone.

cfo_field.q: Read the cash flow statement first. Always.
cfo_field.a: P&L is an opinion, cash is a fact. Open any set of accounts at the cash flow statement, compare operating cash flow to EBITDA over three years, and look at the gap. A business converting 90%+ of EBITDA to operating cash is real. One converting 50% has its profit sitting in working capital or is capitalising something it should be expensing. That one ratio finds more problems than any variance pack.
cfo_field.who: The first thing to check, every time

cfo_field.q: Scenario planning beats a single budget, and costs less than it sounds.
cfo_field.a: Three cases — base, downside, upside — with the two or three variables that actually move the outcome, not thirty. In retail that is usually like-for-like growth, gross margin, and rent renewals. The value is not the numbers; it is that the board has already discussed the downside before it arrives, so the conversation when it does is about the response rather than about whether it is happening.
